INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Joseph Blocher is the Lanty L. Smith ’67 Distinguished Professor of Law at Duke University School of
Law.  His scholarship on gun rights and regulation has
been published in the Yale Law Journal, the Stanford
Law Review, the Harvard Law Review Forum, and
other leading academic journals.  See, e.g., Bans, 129
Yale L.J. 308 (2019); Good Cause Requirements for
Carrying Guns in Public , 127 Harv. L. Rev. F. 218
(2014); Firearm Localism, 123 Yale L.J. 82 (2013); The
Right Not to Keep or Bear Arms, 64 Stan. L. Rev. 1
(2012).  His publications include a forthcoming article
on the  Second Amendment and “common use ,” The
Common Use Test and the Question of Constitutional
Coverage, 125 Mich. L. Rev. (forthcoming 2027).  His
work has also been cited by many federal courts of appeals.  E.g., Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 464 (4th
Cir. 2024)  (en banc) .  His book The Positive Second
Amendment:  Rights, Regulation, and the Future of
Heller (2018) (with Darrell A.H. Miller)  includes a
comprehensive account of the history, theory, and law
of the right to keep and bear arms.  His expertise in
the history of firearm s regulations and familiarity
with lower-court class-of-arms cases render him well
suited to assist the Court in evaluating whether to extend a novel categorical protection to AR-15s and similar weapons simply because they are purportedly
widely owned.

1 Pursuant to Rule 37.6, amic us affirms that no counsel for a
party authored this brief in whole or in part, and that no entity
or person other than amicus and its counsel made any monetary
contribution intended to fund the preparation or submission of
this brief.

2


INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
In petitioners’ telling, there is “an absolute right to
possess arms in common use for lawful purposes.”  Br.
of Pet’rs at 29.  The bare fact that many such weapons
are now in circulation in the States that have not made
them unlawful is, in petitioners’ view, dispositive of
the question whether the Second Amendment bars
any government from prohibiting or materially restricting their ownership or use,  regardless of any
harm they inflict on the public.
That is incorrect.  The Second Amendment  has
never provided an “absolute” right to possess and use
any weapon without restriction , simply because such
weapons are already in general circulation.  See Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. 185, 193 (2026); District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 624- 625 (2008) (describing some weapons, e.g., “short-barreled shotguns,” as constitutionally unprotected ).  And indeed
courts have overwhelmingly concluded that restrictions on AR -15s and similar weapons are constitutional because they fit comfortably within this Nation’s regulatory traditions.  In that regard, amicus
will focus on two overarching points.
First, this Court’s decision in United States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174 (1939) , from which petitioners’ purported “common use” test  derives, does not remotely
support petitioners’ arguments for an absolute Second
Amendment right to possess assault weapons.  T he
Miller Court’s analysis proceeded from the premise
that the only weapons the Second Amendment could
conceivably shield from state regulation were the
weapons citizens would need if called to serve in colonial-era militias —that is, weapons suitable for mili-

3


tary use.  Id. at 178-179.  This Court’s decision in Heller repudiated every aspect of that approach.  It both
protected the right to bear arms for self -defense irrespective of whether those arms would have had any
use in military service,  and emphatically rejected the
proposition that dangerous military weapons could not
be subject to state regulation because such weapons
would be of the type that were suitable for use in military service.  See Heller, 554 U.S. at 582, 624-625.  Accordingly, Miller’s uncritical assertion that the arms
in common use at the Founding were the sorts of arms
suitable for the militia represented the very mode of
Second Amendment analysis that Heller rejected.  It
was also wrong.  Historical analysis  has shown that
weapons in common use at the time of the Founding
were typically unsuitable for militia service.  That is
why Founding -era laws encouraged, and sometimes
even required, citizens to obtain weapons suitable for
militia service.  See infra, pp. 8-10.  It thus makes little
sense to look to Miller—let alone history or tradition—
as authority for  petitioners’ proposed “common use”
test.  See Joseph Blocher, The Common Use Test and
the Question of Constitutional Coverage , 125 Mich. L.
Rev. (forthcoming 2027)2 (manuscript at 21-31).
Second, making a numbers-based “common use”
analysis the sole determinant of Second Amendment
protection would not establish an administrable  rule
for future class-of-arms cases.  T here is no neutral
principle that determines when a weapon is “common.”
Even if such a line could be drawn, it  would be resistant to evidentiary  proof; formulations such as “in
common use for self -defense” are particularly susceptible to variation in measurement, and the set of firearms in “common use” is subject to rapid technological

2 https://perma.cc/8VSB-YLVG.

4


and commercial change .  The test is also circular:  it
protects weapons because they have not been banned,
but it permits bans because they already exist .  That
logic is incompatible with this Court’s precedents overruling handgun bans but allowing restrictions on military-grade weapons.
For these reasons, t he Court should firmly  reject
petitioners’ efforts to create a novel categorical protection for any class of weapons that happens already to
be in circulation.  Although the traditional understanding of “ Arms” or practice of regulating “dangerous or unusual” weapons may involve some consideration of common use or associated factors, that is no basis to make Second Amendment protection turn entirely on a counting exercise.  This Nation’s history is
replete with examples of legislation targeting particularly dangerous weapons  that confer minimal defensive benefit but wreak widespread harm—even when,
and often precisely because,  they are commonplace.
Regulation of AR -15-style weapon s fits well within
that tradition.
ARGUMENT
I. The number of weapons in circulation at a
given time has never conclusively defined
the Second Amendment right.
The Second Amendment is not a right to possess
“any weapon whatsoever.”  Heller, 554 U.S. at 626.  To
the contrary, this Court has recognized that militarygrade weapons and certain other unusual weapons are
beyond the right’s  scope altogether.  Id . at 624- 625,
627.  By the same token, this Court has never applied
a numerical test that categorically protect s any
weapon in general circulation, no matter how novel or
dangerous its characteristics.  See generally Bianchi
v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 460 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc)

5


(Wilkinson, J.)  (“[W]eapons that are not  in common
use can safely be said to be outside  the ambit of the
Second Amendment.  But the logic does not work in
reverse.  Just because a weapon happens to be in common use does not guarantee that it falls within the
scope of the right to keep and bear arms.”).
This Court has thus recognized that the application
of the Second Amendment is not conclusively determined by the fact  that a weapon has already been
banned, or, conversely, by the fact that it has already
entered private circulation .  For instance, new weapons like stun guns can enable the use of nonlethal force
in self-defense, regardless of whether they were widely
available in previous eras.  Caetano v. Massachusetts,
577 U.S. 411, 412  (2016) (per curiam).  And it would
be “startling” to infer blanket Second Amendment protection for military weapons like machine guns, Heller,
554 U.S. at 624—even though there may be hundreds
of thousands of them in private hands , Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives, Data & Statistics3 (accessed Oct. 9, 2026) (“ATF Statistics”).
It would be equally “startling” to apply a numerical
“common use” test (which omits consideration of
whether a weapon is unusually dangerous) to resolve
this case, given that AR- 15s are such close cousins of
M16s—the very military firearms that this Court in
Heller identified as obviously subject to regulatory
prohibition because of how unusually dangerous they
are.  554 U.S. at 62 4, 627.  The weapons are in most
respects identical.  The principal difference between
the two is that the military M16 version is a fully automatic weapon capable of firing several hundred bul-

3 https://perma.cc/R84G-GGV9.

6


lets per minute, while the AR-15 version that is available for civilian purchase and use in States where it is
legal is a semi- automatic weapon capable of firing up
to about 100 bullets per minute—though it can also be
easily modified to mimic fully automatic fire.  The differences between the two weapons “pale[] in significance” compared to the similarities.  Bianchi, 111
F.4th at 454-456.
In nonetheless advocating for a “common use” test
that would conclusively forbid restriction s on possessing or using AR -15-style assault weapons , petitioners place considerable weight on  Heller’s discussion of  United States  v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174, 179
(1939), a decision that included a passing reference to
“common use.”  Br. of Pet’rs at 28-29 (citing Heller, 554
U.S. at 624- 627).  But —as petitioners’ conspicuous
failure to cite Miller itself reflects—that decision cannot possibly bear the weight of petitioners’ argument
or justify adoption of the test they propose.
Miller upheld a ban on sawed -off shotguns by applying the principle that the Second Amendment must
be “interpreted and applied” with the purpose of supporting the States’ ability to call forth the militia.  Id.
at 178-179.  It noted the “absence of any evidence tending to show that possession or use” of such weapons
had “some reasonable relationship to the preservation
or efficiency of a  well regulated militia” and withheld
“judicial notice that this weapon is any part of the ordinary military equipment or that its use could contribute to the common defense.”  Id. at 178.  Then Miller surmised that the colonists would have reported to
service in the militia  with “arms supplied by themselves and of the kind in common use at the time.”  Id.
at 178-179.  The “common use” phrase thus was more

7


literary detour than historical analysis; it had no supporting citation.  And certainly n othing in Miller
turned on whether the weapons at issue were indeed
in common use; the opinion provided no further exposition or analysis on that point.4
Even more to the point, this Court’s decision in Heller repudiated virtually every element of the Miller
Court’s analysis.  See Heller, 554 U.S. at 627-628.  Heller went so far as to describe Miller as “an uncontested
and virtually unreasoned case” “that discusses none of
the history of the Second Amendment.”   Id. at 624 &
n.24.
As particularly relevant here, Heller dismissed any
interpretation of the Second Amendment that would
restrict its protections to “only those weapons useful
in warfare”—rejecting as “startling” the notion that it
could be unconstitutional to impose “restrictions on
machineguns” while allowing regulation of handguns
and other arms typically possessed for self -defense.
Id. at 624.  On the contrary, “weapons that are most
useful in military service * * * may be banned” because

4 The federal government points to a small number of nineteenthcentury decisions purportedly protecting commonly kept arms.
Br. of United States at 13; see also Br. of Pet’rs at 48.  But these
decisions also typically identified the protected arms as “the
usual equipment of the soldier.”  Andrews v. State, 50 Tenn. 165,
186 (1871); Aymette v. State, 21 Tenn. 154, 158 (1840) (“ordinary
military equipment”); Fife v. State, 31 Ark. 455, 459- 461 (1876)
(“such arms as are used for purposes of war” (citation omitted));
State v. Workman, 35 W. Va. 367, 373 (1891) (“weapons of
warfare”), abrogated by N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v.  Bruen,
597 U.S. 1 (2022).  That does not show that all common weapons
were beyond regulation—if anything, it shows the opposite.  See,
e.g., Andrews, 50 Tenn. at 186 ( authorizing effectively
comprehensive restrictions on dirks, sword canes, pocket pistols,
and other weapons).

8


they are not the “sorts of weapons” that the framers of
the Second Amendment intended to protect.  Id.  at
627.  Numerous courts have concluded that AR -15s
and similar weapons may be regulated for this exact
reason.  See, e.g., Bevis v. City of Naperville, 85 F.4th
1175, 1201-1202 (7th Cir. 2023) (“History and tradition leave no doubt that certain weaponry is for the
state only,” such as “grenades,” “machineguns,” and
“artillery pieces” (collecting authorities)); Bianchi, 111
F.4th at 452, 459 (“The Second Amendment, with its
‘central component’ of ‘individual self -defense,’ is not
concerned with ensuring citizens have access to military-grade or gangster -style weapons.” (quoting
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29)).
Heller noted Miller’s dicta about militiamen bringing arms “‘in common use at the time,’” amending it to
add that the arms brought for service would have
needed to be in common use “for lawful purposes like
self-defense” to qualify as arms presumptively protected by the Second Amendment.   554 U.S.  at 624
(quoting Miller, 307 U.S. at 179) ; see also Bruen, 597
U.S. at 21, 47.  But Heller was not primarily concerned
with defining the scope of “Arms,” it did not conduct an
“exhaustive historical analysis,” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 21
(quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 626), and it did not purport
to draw from Miller any rule that weapons in common
use at the Founding (or at any other time) would automatically be protected from regulation by the Second
Amendment.
In fact, the historical record appears to show precisely the opposite of what Miller surmised.  Firearms
in common use at the Founding had minimal  utility
for militia service—militiamen could even be “penalized” if they “turn[ed] up at muster with guns in common use.”  Saul Cornell, The Early American Tradition

9


of Arms Regulation:  Common Law, Common Weapons, and Common Use, 75 Duke L.J. Online 109, 110
(2026).  “The differences between civilian arms and
military arms were well understood by the revolutionary generation.”  Id. at 121.  Firearms commonly used
for hunting were not capable of a sufficient volume of
fire for battle, and they generally could not be modified
to add a bayonet, which would have been critical for
hand-to-hand combat.  Jack Thorlin, Just to Be Safe,
Let’s Keep Ignoring What “Arms” Meant in 1791 , 129
Dick. L. Rev. 1075, 1095-1097 (2025).
Accordingly, Founding-era laws “sought to force reluctant militia members to purchase military quality
muskets equipped with bayonets.”  Cornell, supra, 75
Duke L.J. Online at 120.  Miller itself cited state laws
requiring militiamen to procure specific weapons, confirming that arms were required that were not in common use.  307 U.S. at 180-182.  The Militia Act of 1792
likewise required each militia member to purchase “a
good musket or firelock, a sufficient bayonet and belt,”
and other equipment; the Act also aimed to standardize bores to be “sufficient for  balls of the eighteenth
part of a pound .”  Act of May 8, 1792, ch. 33, 1 Stat.
271, 271- 272.  And t he Act afforded these military -
quality arms legal protections from distraint or execution.  Id. at 272; Cornell, supra , 75 Duke L.J. Online
at 126 & n.87.  “Weapons in common use,” on the other
hand, “were not elevated to any special legal status.”
Cornell, supra, 75 Duke L.J. Online at 124.
The historical evidence thus refutes the premise
petitioners seek to extract from Miller (by way of Heller) that all common weapons  would have been protected as “part of the ordinary military equipment” or
to “contribute to the common defense.”  See Miller, 307
U.S. at 178.  T here would have been minimal benefit

10


from having men report to service  with firearms in
common use for private purposes such as hunting that
could not take a bayonet; the militia laws in fact aimed
to secure the opposite result.  In short, Miller’s historically inaccurate observation  about “common use” is
inconsistent with its own reasoning  and played no
load-bearing role in  either Miller itself or in Heller.
There is thus no reason to elevate it into a rule of categorical protection now .  Nothing about Miller’s reasoning supports petitioners’ demand for a determinative “common use” test for Second Amendment protection.
II. Making “common use” dispositive  of constitutional protection would be unhelpful
for resolving other class-of-arms cases.
Establishing a principle of categorical protection
for weapons in “common use” would also present significant problems as a rule for future class-of-arms
cases.  See Blocher, The Common Use Test , supra
(manuscript at 32-40).
A “common use” test would be in administrable.  One gla ring problem with making Second
Amendment protection turn on a “popularity test,”
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 460, is the lack of any principled
way to determine when a weapon becomes sufficiently
“common” to qualify for constitutional protection.
The difficulty begins with identifying the question
courts would have to answer.  Is federal constitutional
protection determined, as petitioners seem to suggest,
by the percentage of States currently regulating a
weapon?  Br. of Pet’rs at 10, 35 (“legal in the vast majority of states”).  By the percentage of people who supposedly own the weapon —perhaps according to the
answers of a minority of respondents  to an unrepresentative survey?  Id. at 11, 34 (extrapolating from a

11


survey restricted to gun owners that around 4- 5% of
Americans own “AR-15-style” weapons).  By the sheer
numbers that manufacturers are able to flood into the
market before state and local authorities are able to
assess and respond to the risks posed by the weapon?
Id. at 12-13, 35.  And does it matter if a large number
of the weapons are owned by a small number of people?  Kim Parker et al., America’s Complex Relationship with Guns , Pew Rsch. Ctr.  22 (June 22, 2017) 5
(29% of gun owners own five or more guns) .  There is
no indication which of these a “common use” test would
or could enshrine as constitutional criteria, or where
the cutoff would be—making the line “impossible to
draw with precision.”  Janus v. Am. Fed’n of State,
Cnty., & Mun. Emps., Council 31, 585 U.S. 878, 921
(2018); cf. Rucho v. Common Cause, 588 U.S. 684, 707
(2019) (lack of “clear, manageable, and politically neutral” standard establishing how much partisan gerrymandering is too much).
Even if the right metrics  could be discerned, t he
threshold for what is “common” cannot be determined
in a principled manner.  Is a weapon in common use if
it is lawful in 15 States but unlawful in 35, if hundreds
of thousands or millions of such weapons are lawfully
possessed in that minority of States?  And if so , why
should the Second Amendment bind the people in a
substantial majority of States to the public-safety regulatory choices of the people in a minority of States?
What if the States are equally divided on the question?
And if the Second Amendment would not bar regulation in those circumstances, why should the answer
here be different, given that the people of eleven

5 https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2017/
06/Guns-Report-FOR-WEBSITE-PDF-6-21.pdf.

12


States—a third of the Nation’s population—have chosen to ban AR-15 sale or possession?  See Br. of Pet’rs
at 10 n.3.  Alternatively, assuming that the proportion
of Americans who own AR -15s is indeed around 4 or
5%, or even 8 %, is that really “common”?  See Br. of
Pet’rs at 11.  How about 2%?  1%?  Cf. Bruen, 597 U.S.
at 67-68 (giving minimal weight to territorial laws applicable to “less than 1% of the American population”).
These questions are fundamental, but petitioners have
no answer to them.
It should be obvious that petitioners’ approach will
invite litigation that cannot be resolved on a principled
basis.  For example, th is Court allowed a constitutional challenge against a stun gun ban with circulation figures in the hundreds of thousands —i.e., less
than .1% of Americans.  See Caetano, 577 U.S. at 420
(Alito, J., concurring in the judgment).  But if that degree of possession amounts to common use, then fully
automatic weapons would be protected as well, with
hundreds of thousands in potential private circulation.
ATF Statistics, supra.  There are even more high-capacity magazines and bump stocks, owing to manufacturers’ efforts to flood the market.  Mike Spies, Newly
Obtained Documents Show How Gun Manufacturers
Swamped the Market With Large-Capacity Magazines,
The Trace (Dec. 22, 2025) 6 (over 700 million high -capacity magazines produced between 1990 and 2021,
despite federal ban from 1994 to 2004) ; Bump-Stock-
Type Devices, 83 Fed. Reg. 66,514, 66,547 (Dec. 26,
2018) (as many as 520,000 bump stocks held by the
public).  And this is all assuming that the pertinent
class of weapons can be easily defined in the first
place—which it very likely will not be.   See Snope v.

6 https://www.thetrace.org/2025/12/large-capacity-magazine-nssf
-gun-study/.

13


Brown, 145 S. Ct. 1534, 1539 (2025) (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari) (“every single AR-15
can be converted to a machinegun using cheap, flimsy
pieces of metal” (citation omitted)); Garland v. Cargill,
602 U.S. 406, 429 (2024) (Alito, J., concurring) (“a semiautomatic rifle with a bump stock can have the same
lethal effect as a machinegun”).
“Common use” would depend on untested evidence.  Even if a principled “common use” line could
be drawn in theory, applying it in practice will prove
unmanageable.  “[T]he data on firearm ownership necessary to evaluate whether the test is satisfied in any
given case simply does not exist.”  Cody J. Jacobs, End
the Popularity Contest, 83 Tenn. L. Rev. 231, 272- 275
(2015).  Making constitutional protection dependent
on how many firearms are in circulation, or why they
are owned, could allow Second Amendment class -ofweapons cases to turn on unreliable  surveys rather
than reasoned legal principles.  Estimates of gun ownership and defensive gun use vary widely, with Professor (and amicus) William English’s 2021 study proposing an incidence of defensive gun use “more than
twenty times higher than estimates based on data
from the National Crime Victimization Survey.”  Deborah Azrael et al., A Critique of Findings on Gun Ownership, Use, and Imagined Use from the 2021 National
Firearms Survey, 78 SMU L. Rev. 239, 251-255 (2025);
see also, e.g., David Hemenway, Survey Research and
Self-Defense Gun Use:  An Explanation of Extreme
Overestimates, 87 J. Crim. L. & Criminology 1430,
1431 (1997).  But that unpublished study has been repeatedly cited as evidence of “common use.”  See, e.g.,
Duncan v. Bonta, 133 F.4th 852, 902 (9th Cir. 2025)
(Bumatay, J., dissenting); Bianchi, 111 F.4th at  518
n.58 (Richardson, J., dissenting); Hanson v. District of

14


Columbia, 120 F.4th 223, 269 & nn.172, 174 (D.C. Cir.
2024) (Walker, J., dissenting).
Untested surveys about “common use” are a particularly unreliable foundation for constitutional protection.  Evidentiary testing is crucial for statistics —yet
amici often make statistical claims supported by studies that have, for example, never been published.  Allison Orr Larsen, The Trouble with Amicus Facts, 100
Va. L. Rev. 1757, 1784-1787 (2014) (noting that much
“extra-record evidence” in amicus briefs would not
“hold up on cross -examination”).  And there is little
reason to think the courts of appeals have substantial
institutional competence in evaluating untested statistical claims.
These problems will be particularly vexing insofar
as “common use” is understood to incorporate abstract
questions like whether a gun is owned “for self -defense.”  It is difficult enough to sift out the multiple
individual motives for owning weapons, but it may be
impossible to determine why the public owns them  in
any legally coherent sense.  The Court has described it
as “hazardous” to invalidate legislation as unconstitutional based on “guesswork” about “congressional motives or purposes.”  United States v. O’Brien, 391 U.S.
367, 383-384 (1968); see also Kenneth A. Shepsle, Congress Is a “They,” Not an “It”:  Legislative Intent As Oxymoron, 12 Int’l Rev. L. & Econ. 239, 249 (1992) (“Individual intents, even if they are unambiguous, do not
add up like vectors.”).  That reasoning applies a fortiori
to “guesswork” about the aggregate purposes of the
hundreds of millions of members of the American public.  For instance, p etitioners (at 11) cite a  survey
where only a minority of 399 AR-15-style rifle owners
cited self-defense as one of their main two reasons for
owning them; the total number was higher for the set

15


of answers including “recreation/fun/sport,” “because I
can,” “because I want to,” and “angers liberals/people
want to ban them/they make other people afraid.”
Emily Guskin et al., Why do Americans own AR-15s?,
Wash. Post (Mar. 27, 2023)7 (capitalization modified).
And though a higher number (around 65%) agreed
that self-defense was one major reason they owned an
AR-15, about the same number (63%) registered the
same agreement with the statement that they owned
one because “[i]t is fun to shoot.”  Ibid.
Some courts have limited protection to instruments
actually used for self-defense in the home, as opposed
to weapons with speculative defensive utility.  Ocean
State Tactical, LLC v. Rhode Island, 95 F.4th 38, 45
(1st Cir. 2024) (“True, one could imagine Hollywood -
inspired scenarios in which a homeowner would need
to fend off a platoon of well -armed assailants without
having to swap out magazines.  But we read Bruen as
requiring us to ascertain how a regulation actually
burdens the right of armed self -defense, not how it
might be imagined to impose such a burden.”).  That is
more concrete, but it, too, is difficult to measure—and
as courts have recognized, there is no chance it would
cover AR-15s and similar weapons, which are seldom
used in actual self -defense.  See, e.g., ibid.; Kolbe v.
Hogan, 849 F.3d 114, 127 (4th Cir. 2017) (“Neither the
plaintiffs nor Maryland law enforcement officials
could identify a single incident in which a Marylander
has used a military-style rifle or shotgun, or needed to
fire more than ten rounds, to protect hersel f.”), abrogated on other grounds by  Bruen, 597 U.S. 1; Barnett
v. Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035, 1051 (7th Cir. 2026) (rare to

7 https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/interactive/2023/amer
ican-ar-15-gun-owners/.

16


use large numbers of rounds or even rifles generally
for self-defense in the home).
“Common use” varies over time.   Any benchmark that could be established for t he “common use”
test would also be subject to unpredictable change.  As
this Court has recognized, neither firearms nor their
role in society is static.  That is why handguns receive
constitutional protection  without regard to whether
they were “considered ‘dangerous and unusual weapons’ in the 1690s,” given that “they are indisputably in
‘common use’ for self-defense today.”  Bruen, 597 U.S.
at 47 (citations omitted).  However, making isolated
“common use” dispositive would expose constitutional
protection to rapid changes over cycles of technological
advance and commercial popularity.
Which firearms are “in common use” is a question
with an answer that constantly varies as new technology displaces previous technology.  The lethality of today’s semiautomatic weapons, particularly in today’s
urban environments, has no meaningful antecedents
before the twentieth century.  Brian DeLay, The Myth
of Continuity in American Gun Culture , 113 Cal. L.
Rev. 1, 35 (2025) (“repeating firearms and high-capacity weapons were much too rare and too irrelevant to
public safety to attract regulatory attention in 1791”).
The weapons commonly used for self-defense at the
Founding—to the extent weapons were used at all —
were not even firearms.  Firearms at the Founding
“were notoriously inaccurate at range, liable to misfire, and had to be muzzle-loaded with gunpowder and
ball before every shot.”  Id. at 15.  They generally could
not be “kept loaded and at the ready for any extended
period.”  Ibid.  Firearms could be used offensively in
settings where their lack of accuracy was a lesser concern, such as hunting or group combat.  But they were

17


rarely used in self -defense or even as instruments of
crime.  Joseph Blocher & Eric Ruben, Originalism-by-
Analogy and Second Amendment Adjudication, 133
Yale L.J. 99, 153- 154 (2023).  Hand-to-hand weapons
were much more useful for such purposes.  Bianchi ,
111 F.4th at 464.  And certainly, Founding -era firearms are no longer widely  used today—which, remarkably, would suggest that under a “common use”
test, the colonists’ own firearms are now unprotected.
Technological changes continued after the Founding, and the nineteenth century saw  especially rapid
change.  At that point , m ass production introduced
single-shot and repeating  pistols to a broad  market
(leading to a wave of armed crime and ensuing gun
control laws).  DeLay, supra, 113 Cal. L. Rev. at 37.
But these weapons had long reload times and typically
“held between three and seven rounds”—a long way off
from the AR-15’s capabilities.  Id. at 38-39.  The later
nineteenth century brought improvements such as effective breech -loading and metallic cartridges , enabling weapons with more capacity , though they still
could not match the power or accuracy of single -shot
rifles.  Id. at 39-43.  And reloading these weapons was
cumbersome, with magazines that needed to be reloaded one by one.  Ibid.
Further innovations with self-loading mechanisms
and detachable magazines changed the landscape
again in the twentieth century , enabling automatic
weapons—which were promptly regulated by the National Firearms Act in 1934.  Id. at 44-47.
As with automatic weapons, the relatively recent
availability of AR -15s was met with regulation.  Perhaps m ost notably, the manufacture, transfer, and
possession of AR -15s and other “semiautomatic assault weapon[s]” was federally banned from 1994 to

18


2004 under the Public Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection Act, Pub. L. No. 103- 332,
§ 110102, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-1998 (1994).  Only after
the ban expired in 2004 did firearm companies begin
to flood the market with AR-15s, employing the Nation’s military conflicts in the Middle East as an “accidental advertising campaign.”  Todd C. Frankel et al.,
The Gun That Divides a Nation, Wash. Post (Mar. 27,
2023);8 see also Annual Share of AR-15 Assault Rifles
in the Total Number of Firearms Manufactured in the
United States from 1990 to 2020, Statista (June 2,
2023).9
Were this case to have come before the Court a
mere 25 years ago, it would have been startling to contend that the illegal-to-possess AR-15 was “popular,”
Br. of Pet’rs at 8 —and even more dubious to assert
that it was in common public use “for lawful purposes,”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 624 —for the same reason that
longstanding federal restrictions on machine guns
have made it unthinkable to describe those weapons
as “in common use.”  See ibid.; Bevis, 85 F.4th at 1199
(“Indeed, most of the AR -15s now in use were manufactured in the past two decades.  Thus, if we looked to
numbers alone, the federal ban would have been constitutional before 2004, but unconstitutional thereafter.” (footnote omitted)).   The same is true for largecapacity magazines, which some have described as
“the most common magazines in the country,” Duncan,
133 F.4th at 892 (Bumatay, J., dissenting) ; like AR-
15s, such magazines were federally banned until 2004.

8 https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/interactive/2023/ar-15
-america-gun-culture-politics/.
9 https://www.statista.com/statistics/1388010/sharear-15-unitedstates-firearm-production-historical/.

19


A “common use” test would be c ircular.  The
“common use” test  ultimately makes Second Amendment protection circular.  It protects weapons because
they have not yet been banned, but permits bans because they already exist.  As the Seventh Circuit has
recognized, “it would be absurd to say that the reason
why a particular weapon can be banned is that there
is a statute banning it, so that it isn’t commonly
owned.”  Friedman v. City of Highland Park, 784 F.3d
406, 409 (7th Cir. 2015).  T hat decision correctly observed that “[a] law’s existence can’t be the source of
its own constitutional validity.”  Ibid.
Such circularity  would leave society without any
recourse in situations (perhaps including  this one)
when unusually dangerous weapons have proliferated
in advance of regulation.  It is obvious from Heller ’s
discussion of machine guns that “certain bearable
arms—such as the M16, the short -barreled shotgun,
the ricin pellet-firing umbrella gun, and the W54 nuclear warhead —are not protected by the Second
Amendment.”  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 460.  It therefore
cannot be the case that “any one of these or similarly
dangerous weapons could gain constitutional protection merely because it becomes popular before the government can sufficiently regulate it.”  Ibid.  Because a
“common use” test would produce precisely these  results rejected by Heller, it cannot be the law.
The advent of modern technologies like AI and 3D
printing makes these questions even more urgent.
New forms of weaponry could achieve wide public circulation at speeds unimaginable even a generation
ago, and well before the people have an opportunity to
assess whether such weapons should be regulated because they are unusually dangerous.  Under petitioners’ view of the Second Amendment, however, State

20


and local governments would be denied the authority
to restrict such weapons if they flood the market before
the democratic process has a chance to reach an informed judgment about what is in the public interest.
See Krystal LoPilato et al., Artificially Assisted Gun
Violence, Everytown for Gun Safety (Sept. 28, 2026).10
“Common use” would be susceptible to manipulation.  Such circularity is reason enough to reject
the test, but it also would encourage the government
and interested parties to manipulate the relevant factual predicates for the test —by preventing a weapon
from becoming common or ensuring that a weapon becomes so.
First, the test  could spur the government to ban
firearms before they can be widely acquired.  “Machine
guns aren’t commonly owned for lawful purposes today because they are illegal.”  Friedman, 784 F.3d at
409.  Attributing the lack of protection for machine
guns to their purported rarity, rather than their lethal
characteristics, effectively makes the 1934 National
Firearms Act the source of its  own constitutionality.
Craig S. Lerner & Nelson Lund, Heller and Nonlethal
Weapons, 60 Hastings L.J. 1387, 1393 (2009) (the test
“empowers Congress to create its own exceptions to
the Second Amendment so long as the Supreme Court
waits awhile before it checks to see whether particular
weapons are in common civilian use”).  A commonalitybased test thus establishes an incentive to keep weapons off the market so that they do not become common.

10 https://everytownresearch.org/report/artificially-assisted-gunviolence-chatbot-risks-and-preventative-steps-for-responsible-aicompanies/.

21


Second, the test would encourage manufacturers to
inundate the market with weapons before the legislative process can evaluate whether they are dangerous.
As explained previously, supra, p. 18, the firearms industry has proven with AR -15s that it can “flood the
market with new, deadlier weapons in a very short
time frame.”  Jacobs, supra, 83 Tenn. L. Rev. at 268.
Such manufacturing figures can then be used as purported proof of “common use,” given how difficult it is
to track actual private usage.  Ibid.
Third, the test could shield weapons that are especially favored by criminals .  After all,  one reason to
regulate weapons is that their common use presents a
broad threat to public safety and law enforcement .
The “Tommy gun,” for instance, was “all too common
in Chicago”  during Prohibition, “but that popularity
didn’t give it a constitutional immunity from the federal prohibition enacted in 1934.”  Friedman, 784 F.3d
at 408; Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 469 (“As a criminal’s
weapon, the Tommygun was an unqualified success.”
(citation omitted) ).  Similarly, the long-range power
and precision of the Barrett .50 caliber semiautomatic
sniper rifle has “very limited ability to serve the defensive needs of the average citizen” but “extraordinary
capability to advance the offensive purposes of criminals, terrorists, and soldiers”—which is exactly why it
is in common use by Mexican drug cartels.  Bianchi ,
111 F.4th at 453.  And the instant case frames the issue squarely, given that “the AR -15 and similar assault rifles” are “the most popular arms for terrorist
attacks in the United States.”  Id.  at 456-457.  Surely
this is not the kind of common usage that the framers
of the Second Amendment could have intended to safeguard.

22


Limiting the test by requiring common use for
“lawful purposes” is not a feasible solution.  Heller, 554
U.S. at 625.  A sking whether a weapon is sufficiently
“lawful” to be constitutionally protected  verges on
question-begging and raises significant concerns of judicial policymaking.  In a Second Amendment class-ofarms challenge, the entire premise of the suit is that
the legislature has found that a weapon should not be
legal.  Judges should not need to displace that legislative decision by reasoning  that a weapon is or is not
“lawful” in some abstract sense that disregards the decisions of the people’s representatives , without the
guidance of substantive constitutional principles.  See
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 803 (2010)
(Scalia, J., concurring) (rejecting “an assumption that
judges can distinguish between a proper  democratic
decision to leave things alone (which we should honor),
and a case of democratic market failure (which we
should step in to correct)”).
Protection of AR -15s as weapons “in common
use” could have wider consequences .  T he Court
should also bear in mind the wider impacts of class-ofarms decisions under its Second Amendment jurisprudence—in particular, the fact that protection  for AR-
15s is likely to extend a presumptive right to carry
them around this Nation’s densest cities .  Bruen, 597
U.S. at 24.  If a State wants to protect its citizens from
the terrifying sight of mass -shooting weapons near
schools or train stations or places of worship , it will
have to litigate that choice—and may lose.  Bruen, 597
U.S. at 31 (stating that “there is no historical basis” to
“declare the island of Manhattan a ‘sensitive place’
simply because it is crowded”).  A State may not even
be able to protect owners and patrons of convenience
stores or nightclubs by establishing a default rule pre-

23


venting such weapons from being taken inside.  Wolford, 609 U.S. at 190 -191.  The Second Amendment
should not be understood to command that kind of “a
terror to the people.”  State  v. Langford, 10 N.C. 381,
383-384 (1824) (citation omitted).
III. The Court should not recast traditional restrictions on “dangerous or unusual”
weapons into a categorical protection for
weapons in common circulation.
Heller connected “common use” to the tradition of
regulating unusually dangerous weapons, 554 U.S. at
627—but extending categorical protection to any and
all weapons in general circulation at an arbitrary
point in time would not be a faithful interpretation of
that association.
Petitioners claim  “an absolute right to possess
arms in common use for lawful purposes.”  Br. of Pet’rs
at 29.  But “while the founding generation cherished
the Second Amendment right, they did not think it
was absolute.”  Wolford, 609 U.S. at 193.  Even assuming, as p etitioners propose (at 26), that AR -15s are
“Arms” according to the Second Amendment’s text because they are firearms —reasoning that would apply
equally to fully automatic  or ricin-firing weapons—
such arms are subject to traditions of regulation.  See
Wolford, 609 U.S. at 213-214 (Barrett, J., concurring)
(“While history is relevant to both steps” of Bruen , “it
plays a different ‘rol[e]’ at each one.” ( citation omitted)).  Such r egulatory traditions, including restrictions on unusually dangerous weapons, may be
relevant to “help delineate the contours” of the Second
Amendment right and determine “if a challenged regulation fits within that tradition” —even if there is no
“historical twin.”  United States v.  Rahimi, 602 U.S.
680, 691-692 (2024).  T he key question is whether a

24


regulation “comport[s] with the principles underlying
the Second Amendment.”  Id. at 692.
Framing the inquiry as described in Rahimi, it becomes apparent that the tradition of restricting “dangerous or unusual” arms cannot be collapsed into a tradition of restricting only weapons that are not widely
owned.  See Br. of Pet’rs at 49 (“because the banned
rifles are in common use, they are not unusually dangerous”).  The relevant principle—preventing the outsize harms caused by unusually dangerous weapons—
does not hinge on bare numbers.
Limitations on carry of “dangerous or unusual
weapons” were part of the common law,  reflected in
such offenses as going armed.  4 William Blackstone,
Commentaries 148-149 (1769) ; see also Bruen, 597
U.S. at 43-44.  Before the nineteenth century, technological limits on firearms  meant fewer occasions of
armed interpersonal violence.  See supra, pp. 16- 17.
But it is clear that communities could and did restrict
unusually dangerous arms for the  protection of  the
public, and the fact that a weapon might be ordinary
in a rural setting did not make it appropriate in town.
Joseph Blocher, Firearm Localism, 123 Yale L.J. 82,
112-114 (2013).  Urban regulation of gunpowder—i.e.,
explosives—was similarly considered a core exercise of
the police power , even though gunpowder was also
generally used and important for the community’s defense.  Id.  at 115- 116; see, e.g. , People v. Sands, 1
Johns. 78, 79-80 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1806).
Once more dangerous weapons entered circulation
in the nineteenth century,  there are abundant examples of those weapons being regulated —and the fact
that a weapon was in “common use” often motivated
such regulation rather than precluding it.  See generally Repository of Historical Gun Laws, Duke Ctr. for

25


Firearms L.11 (accessed Oct. 24, 2026) (352 results for
nineteenth-century “categorical bans”).  Bowie knives,
with their large blades and sharp edges,  provide a
ready illustration.  The knives were “both widespread
and used for lawful purposes” starting in the 1830s.
Barnett, 180 F.4th at  1047.  Accounts from the midnineteenth century attest to “[t]he popularity of these
weapons as tools of self -defense.”  Cornell, supra, 75
Duke L.J. Online at 130; see, e.g., Cockrum v. State, 24
Tex. 394, 403 (1859) (heightened punishment for use
of “a bowie- knife, the most deadly of all weapons in
common use”) .  Yet their dangerousness prompted
“ubiquitous” regulation. Pet. App.  (25-566) 52a-57a;
see, e.g., Haynes v. State, 24 Tenn. 120, 122 (1844)
(“The design of the statute was to prohibit the wearing
of bowie-knives * * * which the experience of the country had proven to be extremely dangerous and destructive to human life.”).  Such regulations were sustained
on the power of the State legislatures  to “protect our
citizens from the terror which a wanton and unusual
exhibition of arms might produce.”  Aymette, 21 Tenn.
at 159.
This Court should avoid reducing this longstanding
practice of regulating unusually dangerous weapons
into a “dangerous and unusual” formulation that  requires a regulated weapon to be both “dangerous” and,
separately, “unusual.”  Heller’s reference to “dangerous and unusual” weapons , 554 U.S. at 627,  was apparently a misquotation of Blackstone.  Although some
authorities used that phrasing, Blackstone described
restrictions relating to  “dangerous or unusual” weapons.  4 William Blackstone, Commentaries 148-149
(1769) (emphasis added).  Th is formulation was also

11 https://firearmslaw.duke.edu/repository-of-historical-gun-laws/
advanced-search.

26


employed in judicial decisions.  See, e.g. , O’Neill v.
State, 16 Ala. 65, 67 (1849); State v. Lanier, 71 N.C.
288, 289 (1874).
Rather, “dangerous or unusual” and “dangerous
and unusual”  appear to reflect  a single  principle—
along the lines of “uncommonly dangerous .”  Hanson,
120 F.4th at 238 n.7; see also Barnett, 180 F.4th at
1047 (widely accepted “set of historical regulations imposing targeted restrictions on weapons whose danger
and lethality stand out”);  Pet. App. (25 -566) 30a-33a
(“Unusually dangerous  is the obvious fit to describe
weapons that are so lethal that legislators have presumed that they are not used or intended to be used
for lawful purposes, principally individual self -defense.”); Samuel L. Bray, “Necessary and Proper” and
“Cruel and Unusual”:  Hendiadys in the Constitution ,
102 Va. L. Rev. 687, 695 (2016) (“Hendiadys is a figure
of speech in which two terms, separated by a conjunction, are melded together to form a single complex expression.”).  Indeed, a widely used law dictionary employed both the “dangerous or unusual” and “dangerous and unusual” formulations.  Cornell, supra, 75
Duke L.J. Online at 115-116.  This confirms it is inapt
to parse the common-law concept of “dangerous or unusual” as though the phrase were in a statute.  The
formulation can instead be  understood as capturing
the idea that unusually dangerous weapons can be
regulated consistent with a recognition of the right to
keep and bear arms.
A historical tradition of regulating unusually  dangerous common weapons is consistent with the 1700s’
regulation of gunpower by each major American city,
the 1800s’ regulation  of Bowie knives  and similar
weapons by the vast majority of  States, the National
Firearms Act of 1934, the 1994 federal assault weapon

27


ban—and regulation of AR-15s today.  The AR-15 lies
“far outside the animating purposes of the Second
Amendment.”  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 458.  The weapon
has minimal utility for self -defense in urbanized  areas.  Instead, its heightened range and power creates
significant dangers to the public, enabling shooters to
unleash fusillades on unknowing crowds, penetrating
nearby buildings, and reaching neighbors and bystanders—without providing any re cognizable advantage over the arms that are already protected under the Second Amendment.  Ibid.  The burden on the
Second Amendment right from restricting such weapons fits easily within this Nation’s regulatory traditions, regardless of whether they are in “common use.”
CONCLUSION
The Court should affirm each of the judgments below.
